clues.title: Bollard: Bollard
text: The French bollard is extremely recognizable and appears very often. It is a round white post with a pointed top and a reflector band going all the way around. The band can be grey or red. Some rare variations have a fully red top. A bollard that is commonly found in Scotland looks similar, but has a blunt top instead of a pointed one.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Road line: Weird roadlines
text: These middle road lines, where each dash consists of two offset blocks, are unique to France. They are not extremely common, but when you see them, you can safely guess France.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pole: Blue sticker

clues.title: Language: Helpful Words in French
text: Here are a few words in French that can either help you identify the language quickly, be helpful in region guessing, or just help learn the general feel of the language:
**Liberté - égalité - fraternité** the national motto of france "Liberty - Equality - Fraternity"
**Metropole** - Metropolis/City Center
**bois** - woods
**plage** - beach
**la poste** - the post (postal service)
**toutes directions** - all directions
**centre ville** - downtown/city center
**pont** - bridge
**école** - school
**autres** - others
**à louer** - for rent

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Corsican Language
text: On the French Island of Corsica you can find bilingual signs with corsican and French on it. There are also a few signs that only have corsica (if it's only French don't rule out Corsica as that is common as well).
The major language most closely related to corsican is italian. In particular, the endings u/iu/ju, changed from o/io, are common in Corsican.
Example in Corsican compared to Italian:
Sò natu in Corsica è c'aghju passatu i più belli anni di a mio giuventù.
Sono nato in Corsica e vi ho passato gli anni migliori della mia giovinezza.
Note that there are also regional dialects of corsican that have slightly different words.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Direction sign: Basque Speaking France
text: Bilingual signs in Basque, are concentrated In the western half of the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department, bordering the Basque speaking regions in Spain. Common letters include K, X and Z. On directional signs, it’s written with a **thinner font**, which is unique within all minority languages in France.
The word for **street is karrika**, in contrast to “kalea” in the Spanish Basque country.

Basque **is NOT** a romance language but will almost always been seen in conjunction with French or Spanish. Basque is classified as a language isolate (unrelated to any other known languages) and the only language isolate in Europe.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Occitan Language in France
text: Occitan is spoken in the south of France. French will still be the predominant language in this region, but you can see Occitan sometimes on street signs and even more rarely on the town sign as you enter a town.
The best hint is to note the word for "street" in the dialects spoken in Toulouse and Avignon, the two cities where it is most common to see the language (almost always close to downtown).
Toulouse - carrèira Avignon - carreiro
Note that the design you see on these street signs is also unique to their respective cities, even when they only have French.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pole: Ladder Poles
text: In France, these concrete **ladder** poles are pretty common. They're called "ladder" poles because of its similarity to the steps of a ladder.
**NOTE:** Spain can have the same poles, try using landscape or language to tell them apart.

clues.title: Infrastructure - Reddish Road
text: Roads with a significant **red, purple or burgundy** tint are most commonly found in an area between Paris and Dijon, with Normandy being a notable exception. The historical region of Burgundy, which gave the name to the shade of red, roughly corresponds to the highlighted area.
NOTE: Normal roads may deceptively look reddish under some lighting, so use this with caution.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Direction sign: Infrastructure - Dark Green Signpost
text: **Dark green** road signposts and backs are most commonly found in Brittany and around Paris, but also various southern regions in the country.
NOTE: Beware that this, and other colored infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Infrastructure - Eure-et-Loir Sticker
text: Signbacks in Eure-et-Loir may include a green sticker, the department’s logo. They’re usually placed on a dark green back, without a matching post.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Direction sign: Infrastructure - Grey Signback / Green Signpost
text: A **greyish green** signback supported by a **darker green post**, is found in three areas: Brittany (Côtes-d'Armor and eastern half of Ille-et-Vilaine), Pyrénées-Atlantiques and rarely near the Alps.
NOTE: Beware that this, and other colored infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Sign: Infrastructure - Pas-de-Calais Sign
text: In the Pas-de-Calais department, you may find road signs with the following colour arrangement: a **dark green post** paired with a signback of a **lighter shade of green**, ranging from matcha green to greenish turquoise. The department’s logo, a green and blue triangle, is occasionally present on the signback.
NOTE: Under certain lighting, they can appear similar to the greyish road signs. Also, beware that this, and other colored infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Direction sign: Infrastructure - Brown Signback
text: Road signs where both the **post** and **back** are painted **brown** are most commonly found in Seine-et-Marne, and rarely in Ille-et-Vilaine. It is more reliable when the post is **square**, however round signposts are equally common.
NOTE: Beware that this, and other colored infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Street sign: Infrastructure - Cityname Roadsign
text: Street signs in the metropolitan area of Paris often say the **name of the city**, which is generally atypical for street signs in France. The signs will often be made in a **modern design**, and many city names will be **river based**, notably named after Seine and Marne.
NOTE: This can be seen sporadically throughout the country, so consider other clues.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Guardrail: Infrastructure - Cuboid Barrier
text: Cuboid barriers made of **stones** and mortar are commonly found on Corsica. While by no means unique to Corsica, it is good to consider the island when you see them in rounds with a plausible Mediterranean landscape.
NOTE: Stone barriers with a rounded top are not found on Corsica.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: General Architecture
text: French architecture largely consists of stone houses, which will normally be either unpainted or painted in greyish or yellow pastel colours.
The roofs will typically have a simple gable design, with orange tiles or less commonly black slates.

Do note that France has some of the most diverse regional architecture of any European country, so don’t be surprised to see towns that look significantly different from the previously described architecture.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Northwest - Black Shingle Roofs
text: Black shingle roofs are primarily found in the northwest, the rough cutoff being the Loire river.
Other areas include near the Belgian border, the south-centre, and the Pyrenees, making black roofs a good clue for Alps-Pyrenees toss-ups.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Brittany - Architecture
text: Brittany has one of the most recognizable and consistent architectures in the country.
Common elements include, in addition to black roofs, edge chimneys, black slate walls and stones surrounding doors and windows.
The walls will be either very light coloured or made of stone.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: South - Rounded Tiles
text: Roofs in the south of the country will often be made up of rounded tiles overlapping one another, often varying in colour.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Belgian Border - Dark Red Bricks
text: Rows of dark red brick houses, most similar to Flemish architecture in Belgium, are unsurprisingly found near the Belgian border.
The individual bricks may be outlined by white mortar.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Toulouse - Architecture
text: In and around Toulouse, mainly in old towns, you will commonly find bright orange brick buildings.
They differ from brick houses near Belgium by the bricks being brighter, as well as somewhat Mediterranean looking architectural features, such as wooden shutters, being common.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: French Riviera - Architecture
text: The French Riviera will mirror many characteristics of Monaco.

Rich areas with planted palms and light coloured multi story buildings with wide balconies are good indications you’re in this area, with the rest of the southern coast and Corsican Bastia sharing similar vibes.
Just like Monaco, several cities host boat trekkers in their harbour.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Basque - Colorful Timber Framing
text: White houses with, often colourful, timber framing are a staple of Basque architecture that extends beyond the Basque speaking area.
The timber frame colour (in this case red) will be consistent with other wooden elements, like window shutters and gates.
They’re also common in parts of Northern Spain, where the timber frames are usually unpainted.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Alps - Alpine Architecture
text: Alpine architecture, unmistakable for its light coloured base and extensive wooden elements, is unsurprisingly found in the Alps.
Similar houses can be found in the touristic parts of Pyrenees.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Alsace - Germanic Architecture
text: Many elements of Germanic architecture are concentrated in Alsace, such as timber framing and half-hip roof.
Furthermore, roofs with fish scale tiles are more common in this region.
Beware that these elements are sometimes incorporated into architecture in other parts of France, and are most reliable in conjunction with one another.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Paris - Uneven & Cream Colored Stones
text: Walls made of uneven cream coloured to orange stones, glued with mortar and often incorporating red brick details can be found in the towns surrounding Paris.
Note that the city of Paris itself generally does not have this architecture.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - British Hedges
text: Rural roads surrounded by hedges blocking the view, reminiscent of the British Isles, are primarily found in the northwest, particularly in Normandy.
NOTE: Hedges by themselves are not sufficient for recognizing this area and are common all over France.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Vegetation: Vegetation - Stone Pine
text: **Stone pines** are commonly found along the southern coast, often planted alongside urban roads. You may however find them as north as Nantes.

clues.title: Vegetation: Vegetation - Maritime Pine Forest

clues.title: Agriculture - Wine
text: France is the second largest wine producer in the world, with many famed wine regions. The most common include the area around Bordeaux, southern coast and Champagne, East of Paris. Other regions include, but are not limited to, Loire Valley, Alsace and Corsica.

clues.title: Architecture: Architecture - Black Shingle Roof

clues.title: Architecture: Architecture - Brittany Architecture
text: Brittany has one of the most recognizable and consistent architectures in the country. Common elements include, in addition to black roofs, edge chimneys, black slate walls and stones surrounding doors and windows. The walls will be either very light coloured or made of stone.

clues.title: Architecture: Architecture - U-Tiles

clues.title: Architecture: Architecture - Old Toulouse Architecture
text: In and around Toulouse, mainly in old towns, you will commonly find **bright orange brick buildings**. They differ from brick houses near Belgium by the bricks being brighter, as well as somewhat Mediterranean looking architectural features, such as wooden shutters, being common.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Architecture - Ile de France Architecture

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - Cote d'Azur
text: The French Riviera (Cote d'Azur) will mirror many characteristics of Monaco. Rich areas with **planted palms** and light coloured multi story buildings with **wide balconies** are good indications you’re in this area, with the rest of the southern coast and Corsican Bastia sharing similar vibes.

clues.title: Architecture: Architecture - Basque Architecture
text: White houses with, often colourful, timber framing are a staple of Basque architecture that extends beyond the Basque speaking area. The timber frame colour (in this case red) will be consistent with other wooden elements, like window shutters and gates.
NOTE: They’re also common in parts of Northern Spain, where the timber frames are usually unpainted.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Architecture - Alpine Architecture

clues.title: Architecture: Architecture - Germanic Architecture
text: Many elements of **Germanic architecture** are concentrated in Alsace, such as **timber framing** and half-hip roof. Furthermore, roofs with fish scale tiles are more common in this region.
Beware that these elements are sometimes incorporated into architecture in other parts of France, and are most reliable in conjunction with one another.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Language - Breton
text: Breton is a Celtic language, visually most similar to Welsh. Common letters include d, k, w and the letter ñ, which is not found in French. It is commonly found on the Breton peninsula, with bilingual street signs as east as Rennes and rarely Nantes. The Breton word for street is straed.

clues.title: Language: Language - Alsatian

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Language - Occitan
text: **Occitan** is a Romance language closely related to Catalan that’s sparsely concentrated in the South of France, most often found on street signs in big cities, and very rarely on town entry signs. It can be divided into dialects, each using a slightly different word for street, all similar to Catalan “carrer”. For example, in Toulouse, you’ll find the Languedocian carrièra and in Avignon carriero, in the Provençal dialect

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Language - Basque
text: Bilingual signs in **Basque**, a language isolate, are concentrated In the western half of the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department, bordering the Basque speaking regions in Spain. Common letters include K, X and Z. On directional signs, it’s written with a **thinner font**, which is unique within all minority languages in France.
The word for street is karrika, in contrast to “kalea” in the Spanish Basque country.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Language - Corsican
text: On the island of Corsica, you may find bilingual signs in Corsican, a Romance language that utilises many features found in Italian, like words almost always ending in vowels. In particular, the endings **u/iu/ju**, changed from o/io, are common in Corsican. Moreover, placenames will usually have an Italian origin.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Language - Catalan
text: The far southern department **Pyrénées-Orientales**, also known as Catalunya Nord (Northern Catalonia), uses **Catalan** on their various signage.
It is closely related to both Spanish and French, with Ç being considerably more common than in French. The word for street is carrer.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Language - Water Town Name
text: Many French cities contain the name of the river they lay on, usually in the format -sur-[river]. On signage, sur are often shortened to ˢ/, in this case Chalonnes-sur-Loire (Chalonnes upon Loire). The picture shows five of the longest and therefore most common origins of river based names, but cities can bear the name of any river, regardless of length.
Similarly, city names containing -sur-mer (=on sea) or -plage (=beach) are found exclusively on the coast.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Architecture - Mansard Roof

On some occasions, they can also be found in the North of France.

clues.title: France
text: French telephone numbers are 10 digits long, with the first two pairs of digits being two separate area codes, following two patterns:
01 is in Île-de-France and 02-05 goes clockwise from the northwest.
2X is in the far north, with the numbers generally increasing anticlockwise. 9X is an exception, being found both in the far northwest and far southeast.

clues.title: Street sign: Lyon street sign
text: Lyon’s street signs feature four corner bolts and an uninterrupted inner white border that cuts a notch for the arrondissement and each bolt.
NOTE: Outside Lyon proper, the street sign will display the name of the suburb instead.

clues.title: Street sign: Marseille street sign
text: Marseille’s street signs will usually feature the city’s emblem, a variation of the Greek cross. The white border will usually be interrupted at the top, even when the cross is absent.

clues.title: Plate: France
text: Modern French plates are long and white, with blue strips on both sides of the plate. The left strip will be more visible than the right strip.
Some older French plates lack the right blue strip, with the rear plate being yellow. These are very rare in newer coverage.
NOTE: Italian plates also have two blue strips, which are equally visible. In addition, Italian front plates are considerably shorter.

text: Small tables with “Arrᵗ” written on a small separate sign, are found in Bordeaux, despite being a city not divided into arrondissements.

clues.title: Language: French
text: French is a Romance language closely related to languages like Catalan, Spanish and Italian.
The French word for street is **rue**.
French uses these diacritics and special letters:
Accent aigu: **é**
Accent grave: **à, è, ù**
Accent circonflexe: **â, ê, î, ô, û**
Trema: **ë, ï, ü, ÿ**
Ligature: **œ**
Cédille: **ç** with a small hook
In addition, the **-ux** suffix is only found in French.
NOTE: French is also widely spoken in Belgium, Luxembourg, Switzerland and Monaco.
